claim: Traffic signals adapt by gradually increasing green time for approaches with higher traffic flow, creating a self-reinforcing cycle that prioritizes busy corridors
mechanism: Each intersection continuously monitors vehicle count and queue length on all approaches. If an approach shows higher flow than average, its green time is incrementally increased (up to a maximum), while approaches with lower flow have their green time reduced. This creates a positive feedback loop where busy corridors get progressively more green time, while less busy corridors get less
evidence: Myxomycetes reinforce high-flow channels through structural thickening
Traffic engineering principles show that green time allocation affects overall network efficiency
assumptions: Traffic flow patterns are relatively stable over short periods
Intersections can accurately measure and respond to flow differentials
There are no external constraints preventing green time redistribution
expected_failure_modes: Oscillations in signal timing as the system overcorrects
Gridlock if too much green time is allocated to major corridors at the expense of cross-streets
Failure to adapt to sudden changes in traffic patterns
novelty_rationale: This hypothesis applies the principle of positive feedback from slime mold networks to traffic signal timing, creating a self-organizing system without central coordination
testability: Can be tested by implementing the algorithm in simulation and measuring how quickly it redistributes green time after an incident
falsifier: If implementing this algorithm causes traffic to become worse on the high-flow corridors rather than better, as the positive feedback would incorrectly reinforce inefficient patterns
